etymology: Hebrew Shēshān (H8348), perhaps “lily” or “noble,” a man of the house of Jerahmeel in the register of Judah, remembered for having no sons but daughters.
biblical_def: Sheshan was a man of the line of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron, set down by the Chronicler among the households of Judah (1Chr 2:31). His record is brief but pointed: “Now Sheshan had no sons, but daughters” (1Chr 2:34). In a house where the name and the inheritance passed by the sons, this was no small trial; yet the LORD had made provision for such a case in the law given by Moses, that when a man died having no son his inheritance should pass unto his daughter (Num 27:8). So Sheshan, having a servant, an Egyptian whose name was Jarha, gave his daughter to Jarha his servant to wife, and she bare him Attai (1Chr 2:34-35); and from that house came a long line of Judah unto the days of the kings. The dictionary marks two graces in the brief account. First, the inheritance of Judah was kept though the sons failed, for God is not bound by the strength of man. Second, an Egyptian bondman was brought by marriage into the household of the chosen tribe, a quiet foretoken of the day when the stranger and the servant should be made fellowheirs in Christ. Sheshan’s name stands in the book as a witness that the LORD keeps His covenant line by ways past finding out, and forgets none of His own.
webster_summary: A man of the house of Jerahmeel in the register of Judah, who had no sons but daughters, and gave his daughter to his Egyptian servant Jarha.

etymology: Hebrew Zīph (H2128), perhaps “refining” or “flowing,” a son in the Calebite line of Judah, fathered by Mesha (1Chr 2:42); the man, distinct from the wilderness town of the same name.
biblical_def: Ziph is a son in the Calebite branch of the tribe of Judah, named as the offspring of Mesha the firstborn of Caleb: “Mesha his firstborn, which was the father of Ziph” (1Chr 2:42). The reader must hold the man apart from the place, for the same name belongs to the wilderness town of Ziph in the south of Judah, in whose thickets David hid from Saul, and whose men twice came up to betray him (1Sa 23:14-15; 1Sa 26:1; Psa 54:title). The town was very likely named for this man or his house; the genealogy gives us the father, the histories give us the place that took his name. A second Ziph appears among the sons of Jehaleleel in the same chapter’s neighbourhood of registers (1Chr 4:16), a witness to how a name was kept and passed within the families of Judah. The Chronicler does not pause to tell us a single deed of this Ziph; he is content to write the name and pass on. And that is the point of the whole register: the tribe of promise is numbered name by name, generation by generation, that the line might be kept whole unto the coming of Him who should spring out of Juda (Heb 7:14). The LORD knoweth them that are His (2Ti 2:19); even the bare name in the book is precious to Him who writes the book of remembrance (Mal 3:16).

etymology: Hebrew Marēshāh (H4762), “at the head” or “summit,” a man in the Calebite genealogy of Judah named with the founding of Hebron (1Chr 2:42); the man, distinct from the town Mareshah of the Shephelah.
biblical_def: Mareshah is a name in the Calebite branch of Judah, set down where the register turns from Mesha to the building of Hebron: “and the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron” (1Chr 2:42). The reader should hold this man apart from the town Mareshah of the lowland of Judah, one of the cities of the Shephelah that Rehoboam fortified, where Asa met the Ethiopian host of Zerah and cried unto the LORD (Jos 15:44; 2Ch 11:8; 2Ch 14:9-11). The genealogy gives us the man whose house is joined with the founding of Hebron, that ancient and honoured city of the south where Abraham had pitched at the oaks of Mamre, where the patriarchs were buried in Machpelah, and where David first reigned over Judah. The Chronicler is laying the foundations of Judah’s great places by the names of Judah’s men. He does not record a deed of this Mareshah; he records that through him the house ran on toward Hebron, and so toward the throne of David, and so toward the Son of David. This is the labour of the whole register: to keep the tribe of promise named and numbered against the day when our Lord should spring out of Juda (Heb 7:14). The names are written because the LORD knoweth them that are His (2Ti 2:19).

etymology: Hebrew Shēma’ (H8087), “a hearing” or “report,” a son of Hebron in the Calebite line of Judah and father of Raham (1Chr 2:43-44); the man, distinct from the southern town Shema and from the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4.
biblical_def: Shema is a son of Hebron in the Calebite branch of Judah, named with his brethren in the register and then carried forward by his offspring: “And the sons of Hebron; Korah, and Tappuah, and Rekem, and Shema. And Shema begat Raham, the father of Jorkoam” (1Chr 2:43-44). The reader must keep this man distinct in two directions. First, from the place: there was a town called Shema in the south of Judah among the uttermost cities toward Edom (Jos 15:26). Second, and more weighty, from the great confession that begins, in the Hebrew, with this same word — “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4), which the rabbis named the Shema after its opening word, shēma’, “hear.” The man and the confession share a sound but not an office; he is a name in a register, that is a command to all Israel. Yet the two are not strangers, for the whole register exists to keep the people who were to hear and obey the one LORD. The Chronicler writes Shema down because the LORD knoweth them that are His (2Ti 2:19) and forgets no household of the tribe of promise. A name that means “a hearing” is fitly kept among the people called to hear; faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.

etymology: Hebrew Yorqe’ām (H3421), perhaps “spreading of the people” or “the people is poured forth,” a name in the Calebite register of Judah, born of Raham (1Chr 2:44).
biblical_def: Jorkoam is a name in the Calebite branch of Judah, brought forth in the line that runs through Hebron and Shema: “And Shema begat Raham, the father of Jorkoam” (1Chr 2:44). The form of the verse, “the father of Jorkoam,” after the manner of many Judahite registers, may name a man who founded a house, or a place that took its name from him — the families and the towns of Judah being so often bound together that the same word serves for both. Here the dictionary takes him as the figure born of Raham, a single link set down in the genealogy of the tribe of promise. The Chronicler writes no deed of Jorkoam; he is content that the name be kept in its place in the descent. And in this very brevity is the comfort of the whole register, for it shows that the LORD overlooks none of His own. He numbers the hairs of His people’s heads and the names of their generations; not one is lost on the long road from Caleb to the Christ who sprang out of Juda (Heb 7:14). Jorkoam will never be famous among men, yet his name stands written where God has written it, and the LORD knoweth them that are His (2Ti 2:19). The book of remembrance is fuller than any roll of the great (Mal 3:16).

etymology: Hebrew Shammāy (H8060), perhaps “celebrated” or “desolate,” a man reckoned in the registers of Judah, in the line of Jerahmeel and of Caleb (1Chr 2:28, 2:44-45; cf. 4:17).
biblical_def: Shammai is a man of the tribe of Judah whose name the Chronicler records more than once as he traces the households of Jerahmeel and of Caleb. In the line of Jerahmeel he is reckoned as a son of Onam: “And the sons of Onam were, Shammai, and Jada... And the sons of Shammai; Nadab, and Abishur” (1Chr 2:28, 2:32). In the Calebite line he stands fathered of Rekem and father of Maon: “and Rekem begat Shammai. And the son of Shammai was Maon: and Maon was the father of Bethzur” (1Chr 2:44-45). A Shammai is named also among the sons of Ezra in the register of Judah (1Chr 4:17). Whether these be one man set in differing branches as the Chronicler joins the houses, or names repeated within the tribe after the manner of Judah, the dictionary takes him as the genealogical figure of the second chapter. He should not be confused with the later rabbi of that name, who belongs to the age between the Testaments and not to the sacred record. The Chronicler writes Shammai down for the same reason he writes all the rest: to keep the tribe of promise named and numbered against the coming of the Christ (Heb 7:14). The LORD knoweth them that are His (2Ti 2:19), and the names that crowd the register are the names that crowd His book of remembrance (Mal 3:16).

etymology: Hebrew Mā’ōn (H4584), “habitation” or “dwelling,” the son of Shammai and father of Bethzur in the Calebite register of Judah (1Chr 2:45); the man, distinct from the town Maon and from the Maonites.
biblical_def: Maon is the son of Shammai in the Calebite branch of Judah, and the father of the house of Bethzur: “And the son of Shammai was Maon: and Maon was the father of Bethzur” (1Chr 2:45). The reader must hold the man apart from the place, for there was a town called Maon in the hill country of Judah, near Carmel, where dwelt churlish Nabal and where David sheltered in the wilderness of Maon as Saul pursued him (Jos 15:55; 1Sa 23:24-25; 1Sa 25:2). He must also be kept distinct from the Maonites, a hostile people who oppressed Israel in the days of the judges (Jdg 10:12). The genealogy gives us the man whose house founded Bethzur; the histories give us a town and a people who shared the sound of his name. His name, “habitation,” is well set in a register that keeps the dwellings of Judah, for the LORD is Himself the dwelling-place of His people in all generations (Psa 90:1). The Chronicler writes Maon down to keep the line whole toward the city of the great King and the King who should spring out of Juda (Heb 7:14). The LORD knoweth them that are His (2Ti 2:19); the man whose name means “dwelling” dwells secure in the remembrance of God.

etymology: Hebrew Bēth-tsūr (H1049), “house of rock” or “house of the rock,” the eponymous head of the house of Bethzur in the Calebite register, fathered of Maon (1Chr 2:45); the founder/figure, distinct from the fortified town Beth-zur.
biblical_def: Beth-zur appears in the Calebite register of Judah as the offspring of Maon and the head of a house: “and Maon was the father of Bethzur” (1Chr 2:45). After the manner of many Judahite genealogies, the same word names at once a man, the house that came of him, and the town that bore the name; here the dictionary takes him as the eponymous figure, the founder or head of the house of Bethzur. The reader should hold him distinct from the fortified town Beth-zur in the hill country of Judah, which Rehoboam built for the defence of his kingdom and which was a stronghold in the wars of after days (Jos 15:58; 2Ch 11:7; Neh 3:16). The name itself preaches: “house of rock.” The man and the town stood upon the rock of the Judean hills, but the household of faith is built upon a surer Rock. The LORD is the Rock of His people, and there is no rock like our God (Deu 32:4; 1Sa 2:2); and Christ Himself is the Rock smitten in the wilderness and the chief corner stone (1Co 10:4; 1Pe 2:6). The Chronicler keeps this house of rock in the register to keep the tribe of promise whole toward the day when the true House upon the Rock should be built by the Son of David who sprang out of Juda (Heb 7:14). The LORD knoweth them that are His (2Ti 2:19).

etymology: Hebrew ’Azaryah (H5838), “the LORD hath helped” or “whom the LORD aids,” the son of Jehu in the house of Jerahmeel of Judah (1Chr 2:38-39); one of many men named Azariah in the sacred record.
biblical_def: Azariah is the son of Jehu in the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah, set in the descent that runs through Obed and Jehu unto Helez and beyond: “And Obed begat Jehu, and Jehu begat Azariah, And Azariah begat Helez, and Helez begat Eleasah” (1Chr 2:38-39). The reader should mark that Azariah is among the most common names in all the sacred record, borne by many men — a high priest in Solomon’s day, a king of Judah who is also called Uzziah, one of Daniel’s three companions renamed Abednego, and many more (1Ki 4:2; 2Ki 15:1-7; Dan 1:6-7). This Azariah is none of those, but the genealogical figure of the second chapter of Chronicles, a single link in the house of Jerahmeel. His name is a whole confession: “the LORD hath helped.” Set in a bare register of begettings, it preaches the truth that carried the tribe of promise across the centuries: that the help of every household of Judah was the LORD Himself, who kept the line unbroken when no man could have kept it. The Chronicler writes Azariah down because the LORD knoweth them that are His (2Ti 2:19), and the help that named him is the same help that brought the tribe at last to the Son who sprang out of Juda (Heb 7:14). His name is written, and the names of all the helped of God, in the book of remembrance (Mal 3:16).

etymology: Hebrew Yahdāy (H3056), perhaps “whom the LORD directs” or “Jah leadeth,” a man in the Calebite genealogy of Judah whose sons are named in the register (1Chr 2:47).
biblical_def: Jahdai is a man in the Calebite branch of Judah whose household is set down with all his sons named in order: “And the sons of Jahdai; Regem, and Jotham, and Geshan, and Pelet, and Ephah, and Shaaph” (1Chr 2:47). He enters the register without preamble, his connection to the surrounding names of Caleb’s house left unstated; the Chronicler simply joins his household to the others as he gathers the families of Judah. Six sons are reckoned to him, each kept by name, so that a man of whom no deed is told is yet the head of a numbered house in the tribe of promise. His name itself is a quiet confession, “whom the LORD directs” or “Jah leadeth” — a fitting word for a man set in the long descent that the LORD was leading, generation upon generation, toward the Christ. The register is the visible track of an invisible leading; God directed every begetting in it, and lost none. So the comfort of the whole chapter rests on this least-known head of a house: that the LORD knoweth them that are His (2Ti 2:19), and that He led the tribe of Judah by ways its men never saw unto the day when our Lord should spring out of Juda (Heb 7:14). The sons of Jahdai are written, as are all the names of the directed of God, in His book of remembrance (Mal 3:16).
